newsitem.title: HUNGARY: IMF begins overview of stand-by loan to Hungary.
newsitem.headline: IMF begins overview of stand-by loan to Hungary.

text.p: A visiting delegation of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) begins the second overview of a $386 million stand-by loan facility to Hungary on Wednesday, the Finance Ministry said.
"The delegation begins the second review of the stand-by loan agreement concluded this year and closes negotiations about performance criteria for next year," the ministry said in a statement.
Hungary and the IMF signed the loan agreement, which has a 23-month maturity, in March.
IMF officials were not immediately available for comment.

In March, Hungary and the IMF agreed that Hungary should cut its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996, compared with 7.1 percent in 1995, and reduce its current account deficit to $2 billion this year from $2.5 billion last year.
Hungary also said then it did not plan to use the loan facility, but wanted the agreement as a seal of the IMF's approval of its economic policies to reassure investors.

Following the first overview of the loan in July, the IMF said Hungary's main economic objectives could be achieved, but inflation should be reduced further and social security reform needed to be sped up.
IMF directors visiting Hungary a month ago said the economy had achieved considerable progress in the past two years.

Director Willy Kiekens told Reuters then that Hungary's economic growth was likely to pick up if the country continued to reduce inflation and its 1997 fiscal deficit, not including debt service on loans to be taken over from the central bank, fell to three percent of GDP from 1996's four-percent target.
Hungary forecasts maximum GDP growth of one percent this year and two to three percent in 1997.

Kiekens said Hungary should not soften its economic programme in 1997 as it approached elections and should continue economic reforms, including passage of a planned law to reform the pension system no later than March 1997 and further streamlining of the healthcare system.

In October, Standard & Poor's raised its rating for the National Bank of Hungary's long-term foreign currency-denominated debt to triple-B minus, the first time Hungary has received an investment grade from one of the most influential credit rating agencies.
The upgrade was given though it had been clear since the middle of the year that the deficit of the social security funds -- pensions and healthcare -- would exceed target levels.
Last week, Hungary's parliament passed a budget amendment allowing a 1996 social security deficit of 60.1 billion forints, more than three times the original target.
However, the Finance Ministry said greater-than-expected budget revenues were likely to help Hungary keep the budget deficit at the four-percent target.
